title: Suffocating Broncos defense forces Sam Darnold pick in OT, Wil Lutz boots Seahawks
text:
Ja’Quan McMillian, the lynchpin holding together a makeshift secondary, came to the rescue late Thursday night.
Kicker Wil Lutz of the Denver Broncos celebrates his game-winning kick to beat the Seattle Seahawks in overtime on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026, at Empower Field at Mile High in Denver.
Ja’Quan McMillian, the lynchpin holding together a makeshift secondary, came to the rescue late Thursday night. The standout nickel intercepted Sam Darnold in overtime to set the Broncos up for a 17-14 win over Seattle when, moments later, Wil Lutz buried a walk-off, 53-yard field goal.
Denver’s defense, battered by injury and hung out to dry by a moribund offense much of the night, had one last play against the defending Super Bowl champions when they needed it most. Of course it was the undersized slot man who seems to have a nose for the ball. Sean Payton’s team has problems offensively, to be sure. The head coach assuming play-calling duties from Davis Webb after four games did not provide the jolt he hoped.
They can’t consistently run the ball and Nix has not looked comfortable most of the season. All the same, Denver is 4-2 coming out of a brutal six-game opening run that featured Kansas City and five postseason teams from a year ago. They are alive and well in the AFC West and have 10 days to rest before traveling to Arizona on Oct. 25.
Payton likes to say that a quarterback’s two best friends are a run game and a quality defense. Nix had friends early in Thursday night’s game. The Broncos ran the ball on 15 of their first 28 offensive snaps, including short touchdown runs from J.K. Dobbins and RJ Harvey.
They didn’t run with much efficiency or much in the way of big plays in the first half, but they stuck to it and still mounted two impressive scoring drives. First, Nix and the offense went 74 yards over 16 bruising plays and punched in a Dobbins touchdown run at the end of an 8:39 march.
Next time they got the ball, they went back to work, covered 79 yards in nine plays, and put the ball in the end zone on a direct snap to Harvey. Running back RJ Harvey of the Denver Broncos celebrates a rushing touchdown against the Seattle Seahawks during the first half of a game on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026, at Empower Field at Mile High in Denver.
Those two touchdown drives stood up for much of the game because the Broncos defense was rolling from the start. They sacked Seattle quarterback Sam Darnold twice on the game’s opening drive, forced a fumble on Drive No. 4, held star wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba in check for much of the night and controlled the flow of the game.
All of that, of course, with a pair of All Pros missing from their secondary in Pat Surtain II and Talanoa Hufanga and only limited snaps for starting corner Riley Moss , who was dressed for the game but did not play much. When Nik Bonitto generated pressure on Darnold and then defensive tackle Zach Allen finished him off late in the third quarter, it was already the defense’s fourth of ___ on the night.
At that point, Seattle had just 159 total yards of offense and had mustered just 3.5 per play. The Broncos defense did it by getting high-quality play out of reserve cornerbacks Jahdae Barron and Kris Abrams-Draine and rolling personnel through in ways they don’t typically when their health is in better shape. Moss saw snaps here and there.
Devon Key started at safety but Taylor Rapp made his Denver debut and played extensively in the back end next to Brandon Jones. Ja’Quan McMillian did his normal work in the slot, including Denver’s first sack of the night on a well-timed blitz. The Broncos needed that kind of performance, too, because outside of the back-to-back touchdown drives in the first half, Denver’s offense struggled to get anything going.
Cornerback Kris Abrams-Draine of the Denver Broncos breaks up a pass intended fore wide receiver Tory Horton of the Seattle Seahawks during second half of a 17-14 overtime Broncos win on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026, at Empower Field at Mile High in Denver. Payton’s second game calling plays featured just one first down in the third quarter — it came on a play-action completion to Courtland Sutton — and a trio of punts, all of which came while leading 14-3.
Instead of extending the lead or leaning on the clock, though, the three drives combined to cover just 4:40 on the game clock. That lack of production came as Payton tried to open up the passing game and get his quarterback rolling in the third quarter. Over the first 30 minutes, Denver ran the ball 17 times and passed it 15. In the third quarter, Payton called seven passes to just three runs.
Nix entered the fourth quarter 13 of 22 passing for just 93 yards. At that point, he had averaged 1.2 air yards per attempt, according to Next Gen Stats, and had not completed a pass beyond the first-down marker. Nix and company ultimately punted six straight times while playing with the lead in the second half, putting the defense in adverse situations time and time again.
